---
title: "The Price Tag Behind America’s Income Rankings"
date: 2026-10-06
categories:
  - Regional Economics
  - Purchasing Power
  - Data Visualization
---

![](BlogPost04Cover.png){width="500px"}

In 2024, California ranked fourth among the 50 states in nominal per capita 
personal income; South Dakota ranked 13th. After adjusting income for local 
prices, South Dakota rose to fourth and California fell to 12th. No one’s 
income changed because of this calculation. What changed was the yardstick used 
to compare it.

That reversal caught my attention because of a familiar problem in a job search.
If two hypothetical jobs each offered $80,000, they would look tied in the 
salary column. Once I considered rent, groceries, and transportation in each 
location, the comparison would become less straightforward. A state’s average 
income cannot tell me what either job would pay, and a state’s average price 
level is not my personal budget. Still, the example raises a broader question: 
when we call a state “high income,” do we also assume that money goes further 
there? 
**Would the highest-income states still lead after accounting for local prices?**

To examine that question, I compare the [Bureau of Economic Analysis’s (BEA) per capita personal income](https://www.bea.gov/data/income-saving/personal-income-by-state) across 
the 50 states in 2024. The measure includes income beyond wages. For prices, I 
use BEA’s [regional price parities(RPPs)](https://www.bea.gov/data/prices-inflation/regional-price-parities-state-and-metro-area) for the same year. With the national price level set to 100, an RPP 
describes a state’s relative prices for goods and services; housing is only one 
component. I divide each state’s nominal per capita income by its RPP divided 
by 100. An RPP of 110 means dividing income by 1.10; an RPP of 90 means dividing
it by 0.90. The result compares state incomes on a common price basis. It is 
not a measure of anyone’s paycheck.

Both maps use the same color scale: darker states rank higher, though the 
colors do not show how many dollars separate them. On the nominal map, dark 
colors appear in the Northeast and California, but also in Wyoming. Wyoming 
already ranked third, so the original list was never a simple contest between 
the coasts and the interior. On the adjusted map, the middle of the country 
becomes more prominent. Wyoming moves to first, while South Dakota, Nebraska, 
and North Dakota enter the top ten. South Dakota stands out because it began 
outside that group.

![](figures/01_nominal_pcpi_map_2024.png){width="95%"}

![](figures/02_rpp_adjusted_pcpi_map_2024.png){width="95%"}

The other half of the maps matters just as much. California slips from fourth 
to 12th, and Hawaii becomes much lighter. Yet Connecticut and Massachusetts 
remain second and third. Local prices change some important positions without 
pushing high-income states as a group out of the lead. Telling only South 
Dakota’s rise or California’s fall would miss that tension.

The top ten provide a useful check: seven of the original ten states remain 
there after the adjustment. Across all 50 states, 44 change rank, but the 
median absolute change is just four places. “Many states moved” does not mean 
“the whole ranking was overturned.” For a few states, prices substantially 
change the impression given by nominal income. For most, the shift is smaller.

How uneven are those moves? The third figure puts every state on the same 
rank-change scale. Zero means no change; blue marks a move toward first place, 
and orange a move away from it. Iowa and Oklahoma each climb 17 places, and 
Louisiana climbs 13. At the other end, Hawaii falls 26 places, Oregon 15, and 
Florida 13. Six states do not move at all. Hawaii’s long line draws the eye, 
but it does not represent the many shorter lines around it.

![](figures/03_rank_changes_2024.png){width="95%"}

There is another trap in reading this figure: 
**a change in rank is not the size of an income difference**. Iowa climbs 17 
places but still ranks 18th; the chart cannot tell us how many dollars separate 
it from the state above it. Delaware shows why rankings are relative in another 
way. Its overall price level is slightly below the national average, yet it 
falls ten places. There is no contradiction. When all 50 states are reordered 
together, other states can gain more ground and push Delaware down. A falling
rank does not, by itself, mean a state’s prices are above the national average.

These figures also have clear limits. 
**Per capita personal income is an average, not the income of a typical resident or a job offer**; 
it includes sources beyond wages. RPP describes prices across an entire state, 
not the particular city where I might live, whether I rent or own, or what I 
buy. Taxes, school and healthcare quality, commuting, and other aspects of 
daily life are outside this calculation. Finally, these are two rankings of 
the same year, not a record of how residents’ purchasing power changed over 
time. They cannot establish why a state moved.

The two hypothetical $80,000 jobs still have no winner that I can read from a 
map. This analysis answers a narrower question: what do we miss when we look 
only at a list of high-income states? Nominal income is a useful starting point, 
but it leaves out local prices. For most states, turning over that price tag 
moves the ranking only a few places. For a handful, it changes who belongs in 
the top ten.
